proposed_edges.relationship: Liddell Hart attacks documentary and ‘camouflaged’ official military history (1930, 1944)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. The Real War (1930), preface, pp. 9–10 (read in full): ‘a history based solely on formal documents is essentially superficial. Too often, also, it is the unwitting handmaiden of “mythology”.’ Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944), read in part: ‘Nothing can deceive like a document’ and ‘pure documentary history seems to me akin to mythology’ (pp. 8–9); ‘Many are the gaps to be found in official archives’ (p. 9); ‘History that bears the qualification “official” carries with it a natural reservation; and the additional prefix “military” is apt to imply a double reservation. … This camouflaged history … is the dry rot of armies’ (p. 12). His report of an unnamed German general objecting to the Reichsarchiv history’s frankness (pp. 11–12) is his alone. The target is the official-history practice described in Edmonds’s own preface (1922), not a verdict on any one volume; later studies of the British official history (Green 2003; French 1986) are unread. Distinct from edge_562 (Bassford on Keegan), which joins the same pair.

proposed_edges.relationship: Howard judges Liddell Hart’s British Way in Warfare political pamphleteering rather than scholarship (1974)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated: Howard’s 1974 Neale Lecture (The Causes of Wars, p. 172) is unread here and is quoted by Strachan’s 2002 Liddell Hart Centre lecture (read in full), p. 5: ‘A piece of brilliant political pamphleteering, sharply argued, selectively illustrated and [more] concerned to influence British public opinion and government policy than to illuminate the complexities of the past in any serious or scholarly way.’ Strachan adds that ‘The idea of the British way in warfare is not even Liddell Hart’s, it was Julian Corbett’s’ (p. 5), and that the Howard–Paret translation was ‘another breach with Liddell Hart, who had above all been responsible for disseminating that darkness’ about Clausewitz (p. 9). The characterisation of Liddell Hart’s use of history (‘a tool’, p. 2) is Strachan’s. Distinct from edge_561 (Keegan on Clausewitz), which joins the same pair.

proposed_edges.relationship: War economy as war history: Hancock’s civil official histories (1941–49)
proposed_edges.map_label: Hancock: war economy and war history
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated, with exact quotation: Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022, pp. 66–67, read) report that W. K. Hancock headed ‘the civil series of the official history of the war’ from 1941, thirty volumes ‘including British War Economy (1949) which he co-authored with Margaret Gowing’, and quote his memoir Country and Calling (1954, pp. 196–97; unread here): ‘the armed forces nowadays were no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war and their history had no higher importance than that of munition making and agriculture, of shipping, land transport, mining and all the other civilian activities.’ A comparison, not a contribution: the economic-history entry does not list Hancock, and British War Economy itself is unread.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Thin: one mediated statement (Kitchen and Mitchell 2022, p. 16) citing Howard’s memoir Captain Professor, pp. 206–207, which is unread (evidence-1900-1960.md §7e.3). Read the memoir pages first.
No text read (§7e.8); Ritter known from one sentence in Strachan 2002.
The note offers comparison as the alternative when economic does not list Hancock (§7e.4); British War Economy is unread, so the arrow is drawn as a comparison.
Not new edges: evidence added to edge_853, edge_064 and edge_039 through batch.json edge_revisions (§7e.5–7).

new_sources.title: J. E. Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (London: Macmillan, 1922), preface, pp. v–ix.
new_sources.citation: J. E. Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (London: Macmillan, 1922), preface, pp. v–ix.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §1a): the preface, signed ‘J. E. E. April 1922’, in the University of Toronto copy (archive.org militaryoperatio01edmouoft, djvu text). Quoted: ‘THIS history has been compiled with the purpose of providing within reasonable compass an authoritative account, suitable for general readers and for students at military schools … It is based on the British official records’ (p. v); ‘written orders and messages are absolutely reliable evidence of the matters with which they deal, war diaries and reports of actions, written up immediately after events, are liable to contain mistakes’ (p. vi); the ‘Historical Section, Committee of Imperial Defence’, Military Branch, also ‘charged with the sorting and arrangement of the records dealing with operations overseas’ (pp. vi–vii); ‘The French General Staff has not yet issued any history’ (p. vii); material furnished by the director of the German Reichsarchiv (p. viii; OCR corrected); ‘The typescript or proof sheets have been read by a number of commanders and staff and regimental officers who took part in the events narrated’ (pp. viii–ix). The preface documents participant review; its effects on the history’s independence are not assessed here. Green (2003) and French (1986) remain unread.

new_sources.scope_note: The British official history in its own words; ‘from 1922’ dates the first volume, not the Historical Section.

new_sources.citation: B. H. Liddell Hart, The Real War, 1914–1918 (London, 1930), preface, pp. 9–10.

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §1b(i)) in a Digital Library of India scan (archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.57906; OCR corrected in brackets in the research note). Quoted: ‘the time has come when a “real” history of the war is possible’; ‘a history based solely on formal documents is essentially superficial. Too often, also, it is the unwitting handmaiden of “mythology”’; his own limitation, that the war’s decisive impressions ‘were received and made in the cabinets and in the military headquarters, not in the ranks of the infantry nor in the solitude of stricken homes’. The rest of the book is unread.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §1b(ii)): the foreword, pp. 8–9, 11–12 and about 15–16 (folio partly illegible), archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.526495. Quoted: ‘Nothing can deceive like a document’; ‘pure documentary history seems to me akin to mythology’ (pp. 8–9); ‘Many are the gaps to be found in official archives’ (p. 9); a ‘distinguished German general’, unnamed, regretted that frankness had spread to the Reichsarchiv’s official history (pp. 11–12; Liddell Hart’s report only); ‘History that bears the qualification “official” carries with it a natural reservation; and the additional prefix “military” is apt to imply a double reservation. … This camouflaged history … is the dry rot of armies’ (p. 12); military histories ‘usually written by soldiers untrained as historians’ (pp. ~15–16). new_sources.title: Maurice Matloff and Edwin M. Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942, United States Army in World War II (Office of the Chief of Military History, 1953), foreword (p. vii) and preface (pp. ix–x).
new_sources.citation: Maurice Matloff and Edwin M. Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942, United States Army in World War II (Office of the Chief of Military History, 1953), foreword (p. vii) and preface (pp. ix–x).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §1c) in the HyperWar transcription; history.army.mil returned 403. Quoted from Maj. Gen. Orlando Ward’s foreword (5 June 1952): ‘Mr. Snell was formerly an instructor in English at Harvard University and Mr. Matloff an instructor in History at Brooklyn College … Both joined the Operations Division historical project of the War Department General Staff in 1946’; readers should remember that ‘the differences related herein are those among comrades in arms who in the end always made the adjustments required’. From the preface: the project began in 1946 ‘by a group of associated historians, organized by Dr. Ray S. Cline’; ‘Dr. Kent Roberts Greenfield, Chief Historian of the Office and the first and most attentive critic of this volume’; intended readers ‘staff officers, civil officials, diplomatic historians, and political scientists’; Mrs. Helen McShane Bailey’s ‘wide knowledge and exact understanding of the records’. One documented instance of sponsor framing, not a characterisation of the series; Greenfield (1954) and Conn (1980) unread.

new_sources.scope_note: The US Army’s World War II series in its own front matter.

new_sources.title: Samuel Eliot Morison, History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. II, Operations in North African Waters (Little, Brown, 1947), foreword (p. ix) and introduction (pp. xi–xiii).
new_sources.citation: Samuel Eliot Morison, History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. II, Operations in North African Waters (Little, Brown, 1947), foreword (p. ix) and introduction (pp. xi–xiii).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §1d) in a Digital Library of India scan (archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.80804). From the Secretary of the Navy’s foreword: Morison ‘suggested to President Roosevelt’ in 1942 a ‘full, accurate, and early record’; naval activities were directed ‘to make available to Captain Morison such records as he might desire to consult’; ‘This work, however, is in no sense an official history … He has been subject to no restrictions other than those imposed by the necessity of safeguarding information’. From the introduction: ‘I or one of my assistants have visited every theater of naval warfare since 1941, and taken part in as many operations as possible’; ‘No history written during or shortly after the event it describes can pretend to be completely objective’; ‘Historians with military experience will always be more tolerant of failure or lack of success than those without it’; ‘Official reports are not impeccable’. Whether the introduction is the series introduction is unverified; vol. I was not used.

new_sources.scope_note: A commissioned, records-privileged history declared ‘in no sense an official history’.

new_sources.title: David Morgan-Owen and Michael Finch, “The Unrepentant Historian: Sir Michael Howard and the Birth of War Studies,” British Journal for Military History 8, no. 2 (2022): 55–76.
new_sources.citation: David Morgan-Owen and Michael Finch, “The Unrepentant Historian: Sir Michael Howard and the Birth of War Studies,” British Journal for Military History 8, no. 2 (2022): 55–76.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §§1f, 3b, 4b, 6a): pp. 55–67 read; pp. 68–76 keyword-located only (open access, CC BY-NC-ND). Quoted: the War Studies origin story is ‘seductive in its simplicity. It casts Howard as an heroic figure, almost single-handedly … delivering the study of war from the academic wilderness’, ‘a story that Howard himself consciously cultivated’ (pp. 56–57); Laughton ‘a founding member of both the Navy Records Society and The English Historical Review’ (p. 60); Howard’s 1956 article and a 1955 letter to Liddell Hart (pp. 59–60); a 1934 IHR report (p. 61); Maurice’s chair of military studies (1927) and his inaugural lecture, ‘statecraft, economics, the supply of raw material, science, and industry are factors which are of prime importance’, ‘military history is but a special branch of the general study’ (pp. 61–62); the department ‘briefly re-named War Studies in 1943, however it was closed in 1948’, and Howard used Maurice’s lecture for his 1964 inaugural (p. 63); Webster and Frankland’s official history from 1950, Webster ‘convinced … of the relevance and importance of war as a field of scholarship’ (p. 65); Hancock as head of the civil series from 1941, with Gowing, and his Country and Calling (1954), pp. 196–97, ‘the armed forces nowadays were no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’ (pp. 66–67); Hancock among the 1946 Chichele electors choosing Falls over Liddell Hart (p. 66 n. 46, citing Strachan 2014, unread); official programmes ‘catalysed new approaches’ (p. 68, keyword-located). URL supplied at release (release/fixes-1.141.md, finding 12).

new_sources.scope_note: A corrective history of War Studies at King’s and of official history as an entry point for academic historians.

new_sources.citation: Hew Strachan, “Michael Howard and the dimensions of military history,” Liddell Hart Centre for Military Archives annual lecture, King’s College London, 3 December 2002 (14 pp.). Also published as “Michael Howard and the Dimensions of Military History,” War in History 27, no. 4 (2020): 536–551, essentially unchanged according to the coordinating session (not collated here).

verification.note: Read in full for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §§1f, 3b, 6a) as the KCL PDF. Quoted: ‘The dominant figure of course in the field of military history in 1953 was not Falls but … Basil Liddell Hart’; ‘Like Cyril Falls, Liddell Hart was in many ways more a journalist than an academic … For Liddell Hart military history was a tool, a tool to communicate ideas about war that had present application and future implication more than a help to understand the past’ (p. 2); Butler’s 1959 invitation to Howard for Grand Strategy vol. 4 (p. 2); regimental ‘nursery history’ and the ‘myth’; ‘in width, in depth and in context’; ‘Up until Michael Howard’s appointment, almost nobody who had studied the history of war had not themselves experienced war’ (pp. 2–3); closure rules and Ultra (p. 4); Howard’s 1974 Neale Lecture (The Causes of Wars, p. 172) on The British Way in Warfare, ‘A piece of brilliant political pamphleteering …’, and ‘The idea of the British way in warfare is not even Liddell Hart’s, it was Julian Corbett’s’ (p. 5); Ritter (p. 7); Delbrück ‘surely the founding father of academic military history’ and Howard’s preface that ‘paid obeisance to Delbrück’ (p. 7); the ‘new’ military history as ‘the history of war with the fighting left out’ (p. 8); Liddell Hart ‘above all … responsible for disseminating that darkness’ about Clausewitz (p. 9). Howard’s 1974 lecture itself is unread. URL supplied at release (release/fixes-1.141.md, finding 12).

verification.note: Read for the entries 1896–1969 for revision 1.142 (evidence-1900-1960.md §5a). Quoted: ‘1933 March 16; Major C.C. Benson drafts the first position paper calling for a non-profit military history organization to aid the U.S. Army’; the American Military History Foundation incorporated in Washington on 2 June 1933 ‘After a series of informal discussions amongst military and civilian archival personnel’; first issue of its journal 1 April 1937; renamed the American Military Institute (1939); the journal published as Military Affairs from spring 1941; joint sessions with the AHA (1935, 1942) and a 1956 session on ‘The Teaching of Military History: Pro and Con’; a one-year hiatus (1949–50); ‘1957 AMI and Military Affairs near collapse as a result of poor office space, the limitations of an all-volunteer staff and a dwindling membership base’; a temporary office in the Army Library at the Pentagon (1958/9). row.context: Planned a history of the art of war ‘from Greek and Roman times’ (1898), walking battlefields to supplement maps; his Peninsular War (1902) used Record Office papers, including passages omitted from printed dispatches, and treated veterans’ memoirs with ‘very cautious handling’. No influence on or from Delbrück is claimed.
row.works: A History of the Art of War: The Middle Ages (1898), preface; A History of the Peninsular War, vol. I (1902), preface

row.context: A civilian who wrote the army’s history for ‘the political not less than the military aspect’ (1899) and read regimental histories ‘not always with profound respect for their accuracy’. As Trinity College’s first lecturer in military history (1913) he defined it as the strife of communities through ‘organised bands of armed men’, holding that ‘below a certain stage of civilisation, there can be no military history’.
row.works: A History of the British Army, vols. I–II (1899), preface; Military History: Lectures Delivered at Trinity College, Cambridge (1914)

row.context: First Chichele Professor of Military History at Oxford (1909). His inaugural lecture calls military history ‘the effort to understand war’, makes policy, not generalship, ‘the architectonic art’, and holds that ‘as the State is, so will its army be’.
row.works: The University and the Study of War (1909)

row.context: Compiled the British official history of the Western Front in the Committee of Imperial Defence’s Historical Section: ‘based on the British official records’, written partly for ‘students at military schools’, and read in typescript or proof by officers who took part. The preface documents participant review; its effects on the history’s independence are not assessed here. Green (2003) and French (1986) remain unread.
row.works: Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (1922), preface

row.context: Called history ‘based solely on formal documents’ ‘essentially superficial’ (1930) and official ‘camouflaged history’ ‘the dry rot of armies’ (1944), while placing the war’s decisive history in ‘the cabinets and in the military headquarters’. Strachan (2002) calls him ‘in many ways more a journalist than an academic’, for whom military history was ‘a tool’.
row.works: The Real War, 1914–1918 (1930), preface; Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944)

row.context: A Harvard historian who proposed a naval history of the war to Roosevelt in 1942 and was given the records he wished to consult; he or his assistants took part in operations. The Navy declared the work ‘in no sense an official history’; Morison held that historians with military experience ‘will always be more tolerant of failure’.
row.works: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. II, Operations in North African Waters (1947), foreword and introduction

row.context: A former Brooklyn College history instructor who, with Edwin M. Snell, wrote the US Army’s volume on coalition strategic planning; both had served in the war and joined the War Department’s historical project in 1946. The Chief of Military History’s foreword asks readers to see its controversies as differences ‘among comrades in arms’.
row.works: With Edwin M. Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953)

row.context: Chief Historian of the US Army’s Office of the Chief of Military History, named by Matloff and Snell as ‘the first and most attentive critic’ of their volume. A named editorial role only; his The Historian and the Army (1954) is unread.
row.works: Chief Historian’s review of Matloff and Snell (1953), as acknowledged in their preface

row.context: Headed the civil series of the British official history of the Second World War from 1941; as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch, he concluded that the armed forces were ‘no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’. An elector who chose Falls over Liddell Hart for the Chichele chair in 1946. Known here through that article only.
row.works: With Margaret Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Country and Calling (1954), pp. 196–97, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022)

row.context: Appointed to King’s College London’s new chair of military studies in 1927. His inaugural lecture, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch, made statecraft, economics, industry and civilian morale part of the study of war and called military history ‘but a special branch of the general study’; Howard used it to structure his 1964 professorial lecture.
row.works: “On the Uses of the Study of War” (inaugural lecture, 1927), as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022)

row.context: Wanted a ‘science of war’ on which a true history of war would rest (‘We do not want drama; we want truth’) and dismissed Clausewitz’s work as ‘a cloud of flame and smoke’ (1926): history used as a base for theory.
row.works: The Foundations of the Science of War (1926), ch. I §1

row.context: A theorist-historian who used history to argue present policy. Howard (1974, as quoted by Strachan) judged The British Way in Warfare ‘brilliant political pamphleteering’; Strachan credits the idea to Corbett and holds Liddell Hart responsible for ‘disseminating’ English-language ‘darkness’ about Clausewitz.
row.works: The Real War (1930); Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944); The British Way in Warfare, as judged by Howard (1974)

row.context: Co-author with Hancock of British War Economy (1949), in the civil series of the British official history of the Second World War, as Morgan-Owen and Finch report. Known here through that report only; the book is unread and no argument of hers is assessed.
row.works: With W. K. Hancock, British War Economy (1949), as reported by Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022)

row.context: Records work acknowledged by Matloff and Snell: ‘Nearly every page in the volume bears some mark of Mrs. Bailey’s wide knowledge and exact understanding of the records kept by the War Department’. An acknowledgement of records labour; no work of her own is assessed.
row.works: Records assistance acknowledged in Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953), preface

row.context: Acknowledged by Matloff and Snell for assembling the volume’s statistics. An acknowledgement only; no work of her own is assessed.
row.works: Statistical work acknowledged in Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953), preface
